content.title: About
content.content: Cashews are the edible seeds of the cashew tree (Anacardium occidentale), native to tropical regions of Africa and South America. The nuts have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a buttery texture. Cashews are eaten raw, roasted, salted, or as a paste, and are used in sauces, desserts, and vegan dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cashew grows on a tree that produces a fruit (the cashew apple) and the nut hangs from the bottom of the fruit in a shell.
The seed is covered by a soft skin that is usually removed before consumption.
Only the fully ripened fruit is safe to eat; the raw shell contains urushiol, a toxic compound removed during processing.
Cashews are commonly used to make cashew oil, cashew butter, and vegan cheese alternatives.
A mature cashew tree can reach up to 12 meters tall and remain productive for up to 30 years.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: Cashews contain primarily monounsaturated fatty acids, which support heart health.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in cashews helps maintain normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Contains copper and iron
items.content: Cashews provide copper and iron, essential for hemoglobin formation and energy metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The nuts are a good source of B1, B6, and folate, supporting metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Protein and fiber
items.content: Cashews supply plant protein and dietary fiber, promoting satiety and digestive health.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Cashews can trigger allergic reactions, potentially severe, in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Cashews are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Raw toxicity
items.content: Raw cashews contain urushiol, a toxic resin; therefore, commercial cashews are always heat‑treated.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: Whole cashews can pose a choking risk for young children; finely chopped or ground nuts are recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cashews can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, oatmeal, yogurt, baked goods, or blended into cashew butter. They are also used in sauces, curries, and vegan cheese recipes. Soaking them for a few hours softens the texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cashews in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation. Discard nuts that smell rancid or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken wings are a staple item in fast‑food and restaurant menus. They are usually deep‑fried and served with a variety of sauces or seasonings such as barbecue, hot chili, honey‑mustard, garlic aioli, and many others.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wings are often called "wings" and have become a symbol of American street food.
The most famous wing event is the Buffalo Wing Festival in Buffalo, where the original Buffalo sauce was created.
In the United States more than 1.3 billion servings of chicken wings are consumed each year.
Wings can be prepared not only by deep‑frying but also by baking, grilling, or air‑frying.
A wide range of sauces allows the dish to be adapted to any taste preference—from sweet to extremely spicy.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken meat provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Wings contain virtually no carbs, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Wings provide iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood health and bones.

items.title: Antioxidant properties of sauces
items.content: Some sauces (e.g., garlic or ginger based) add antioxidants that enhance the dish’s overall benefit.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Deep‑fried wings are rich in saturated fat and calories, so they should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Spicy sauces
items.content: Hot sauces can irritate the stomach and esophagus in people with sensitive gastrointestinal tracts.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to chicken proteins.

items.title: Salt in sauces
items.content: Many sauces contain a lot of sodium, which may raise blood pressure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wings are typically served hot, with the meat pulled off the bone. They are eaten with the hands, dipped in sauce, and optionally sprinkled with extra seasoning. Common side dishes include fries, onion rings, and fresh vegetable sticks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cooked fried wings should be stored in the refrigerator for no more than 2‑3 days in an airtight container. They can be reheated in an oven or microwave. Raw frozen wings keep for up to 6 months.

fish-sandwich-fried-on-wheat-bun-with-ch.title: Fish sandwich, fried, on wheat bun, with cheese

content.title: About
content.content: The fish sandwich, fried, on a wheat bun, with cheese, consists of a breaded piece of fish that is deep‑fried until golden, placed between a split wheat bun and topped with melted cheese. It is often served with tartar sauce, fresh vegetables, and fries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first fish sandwich appeared in the United States in the early 1920s as a lighter alternative to meat burgers.
A crisp coating is achieved by dipping the fish in a batter of flour, eggs, and spices before frying.
Wheat buns give the sandwich a soft texture and a subtle nutty flavor.
Melted cheese is usually a processed slice because it melts evenly and forms a smooth layer.
Some regional recipes add curry or paprika to the batter for extra zest.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Fish, especially marine varieties, provides EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: One sandwich delivers about 20 g of high‑quality protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D in fish aids calcium absorption and boosts the immune system.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Melted cheese adds calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Fiber from the bun
items.content: The wheat bun provides a modest amount of dietary fiber that helps digestion.

items.title: Fish or dairy allergy
items.content: People allergic to fish or dairy proteins may experience reactions when eating this sandwich.

items.title: High in fats and calories
items.content: Frying and cheese increase the calorie count; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt in the batter and sauces can raise sodium intake, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Possible contaminants in fish
items.content: Certain fish species may contain mercury; choose reputable suppliers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich hot, right after frying, so the cheese is fully melted. Add fresh lettuce, tomato slices, cucumber, or pickled onions for extra crunch. For a lighter version, use baked fish instead of fried.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The sandwich is best enjoyed immediately. If needed, wrap it tightly in plastic film and refrigerate for up to 24 hours. Store fried fish separately in an airtight container, and keep the bun in a dry place to prevent it from becoming soggy.

content.title: About
content.content: Fried tilapia fillet is a tender white-fleshed freshwater fish coated in a crispy golden crust. Tilapia has a mild flavor that pairs well with a variety of spices and sauces. It is usually pan‑fried or deep‑fried and served as a standalone dish or added to salads, sandwiches, and Asian‑style meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tilapia is one of the fastest‑growing farmed fish species, cultivated in more than 50 countries.
Unlike many marine fish, tilapia thrives in fresh water, making its farming relatively simple.
Tilapia is sometimes called “the aquarium fish” because it can be kept easily in home tanks.
Several species exist, but the most common commercial variety is Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus).
High‑heat frying locks in protein and creates a flavorful, crunchy exterior.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Tilapia provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other fish, tilapia contains relatively little saturated fat, fitting well into low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Tilapia offers phosphorus, selenium, and potassium, beneficial for bones, antioxidant defense, and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Its soft texture and moderate fat content make it gentle on the digestive system, suitable for children and older adults.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including tilapia.

items.title: Omega‑6 fatty acids
items.content: Tilapia is higher in omega‑6 than omega‑3 fatty acids, so regular consumption should be balanced with omega‑3 sources.

items.title: Farming quality
items.content: Poor aquaculture practices can lead to antibiotic or chemical residues in the fish.

items.title: Frying oil
items.content: Repeatedly heated oil can generate trans fats; it is best to fry with fresh oil.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the fried fillet hot, seasoned with salt, pepper, or your favorite spice blend. It works well in salads, tacos, sandwiches, and as a filling for sushi rolls. A squeeze of lemon, tartar sauce, or soy sauce enhances the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fried tilapia in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a zip‑top bag at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 2 months. Reheat in the oven or skillet to restore crispness before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Peruvian dried beans (2154) are sun‑dried beans cultivated in the high‑altitude regions of Peru. They have a firm texture, a nutty aroma and a mildly sweet flavor. Beans are commonly used in stews, soups, salads and as a base for plant‑based protein dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peruvian beans are traditionally grown at elevations above 2,000 m, which gives them a distinctive taste.
In Peru the beans are a staple of the national cuisine and are often served with corn and potatoes.
Dried beans can be stored for up to a year when kept in proper conditions, retaining their nutritional value.
Beans are rich in plant protein, iron and fiber, making them valuable for vegetarian diets.
Traditionally beans are soaked in cold water for 8–12 hours before cooking to reduce cooking time.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beans provide a substantial amount of plant‑based protein, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Iron from beans contributes to normal hemoglobin formation and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, increases satiety and supports gut health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Beans raise blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B6 and folate in beans support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in excess.

items.title: Need for soaking
items.content: Raw dried beans contain antinutrients; they should be soaked and thoroughly cooked to avoid digestive issues.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak dried beans in cold water for 8–12 hours, then boil until tender (usually 45–60 minutes). Add them to soups, stews, salads, mash them, or use as a base for vegetarian patties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored they keep quality for up to 12 months. Discard beans that develop a moldy smell or discoloration.
